To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pattern of myocardial cell death in ischemia involves cell swelling, loss of plasma membrane integrity, and rupture of the swollen cells with coagulation necrotic features.

the morphological features of myocardial cell death in ischemia are those of coagulation and that the morphological findings are consistent with the underlying membrane alterations that occur in ischemic myocytes.

the mechanisms of ischemic injury to the myocardium involve membrane dysfunction with the loss of membrane integrity, and that the loss of membrane structure and function results from the depletion of ATP and other high-energy compounds, and the accumulation of Ca2+.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cellular and molecular basis for myocardial cell death and the development of myocardial infraction in response to coronary occlusion.
the elucidation of the mechanisms of myocardial ischemia, the development of myocardial infraction, and the pathogenesis of ischemic heart disease.
the cellular and sub-cellular mechanisms of myocardial injury and death in ischemic and reperfusion injury.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the morphologic features of myocardial cell damage and death are well established.

myocardial cell injury is characterized by reversible and irreversible cell injury, with cell swelling and membrane damage and death, and that these features are associated with the evolution of myocardium infarction.
myocardial cell death in ischemia involves a complex pattern of cell injury that includes membrane damage, cell swelling, and coagulation necroses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the pathogenesis of ischemic injury to cardiac myocytes involves a series of sequential events that include (1) a decrease in the supply of energy substrate and O2, (2) a decrease in ATP production, (3) impairment of membrane structure and function with loss of membrane potential, and (4) the development of a membrane permeability defect.1 The development of a permeability defect in ischemic myocytes has been demonstrated by a number of investigators.1 4 5 6
the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarctions by nuclear imaging is based on the detection of irreversible ischemic cell injury.

the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarct by the pathologist or nuclear cardiology methods is based on evidence of cell injury and cell swelling, and the diagnosis of acute infarct by cardiac enzymes is based on the release of cardiac myocyte proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single mode of cell injury and cell loss in the heart.
the heart is a very dynamic organ, and that it has to be able to adapt to different conditions.
the ischemic myocardium undergoes a series of progressive alterations that involve cell injury and death.
